what-is-nep-2020-for-parents:
India's National Education Policy 2020 in plain language: the structure, what it says about language and assessment, and what has actually changed so far, which is less than the coverage suggests.

The structural change

The old 10+2 arrangement is replaced by 5+3+3+4, and the significant part is that it now begins at three rather than six.

Foundational, ages 3 to 8. Three years of pre-school plus classes 1 and 2. Play-based and activity-based, with formal academics deliberately delayed.

Preparatory, ages 8 to 11. Classes 3 to 5. Play and discovery continuing, with more formal structure appearing.

Middle, ages 11 to 14. Classes 6 to 8. Subject teaching, and vocational exposure introduced including an internship.

Secondary, ages 14 to 18. Classes 9 to 12, with subject choice made considerably more flexible.

What matters most for a parent

Foundational literacy and numeracy is the stated priority. The policy is unusually direct that a large proportion of children reach later years without securely reading or handling number, and that everything else is undermined by it.

Mother tongue as medium of instruction, where possible, until at least class 5. The reasoning is well supported: children learn concepts faster in a language they think in. In practice this is complicated by parental demand for English and by genuinely multilingual households.

The rigid streams are gone. No hard separation between science, commerce and arts. A student can combine physics with music.

Assessment is meant to shift from memorisation towards understanding and application, with board examinations made lower-stakes.

Vocational education from class 6, framed as removing the status distinction between academic and practical work.

Coding from class 6, and computational thinking earlier.

What has actually changed

The honest answer: unevenly, and less than the announcements suggest.

Education is a concurrent subject in India, so implementation depends on states, and states have moved at very different speeds. Some have adopted the structure, some have resisted the language provisions, and some have done little.

New curriculum frameworks and textbooks are being rolled out gradually. Teacher training at the scale required is the largest constraint and is not solved.

For most families, day-to-day schooling has changed less than the coverage implies.

The debates worth knowing about

The language provision is genuinely contested, both on practical grounds and politically. Funding has not matched the policy's own targets. And there is reasonable concern that early vocational streaming could entrench rather than remove status distinctions.

What to do with all this

Ask your school specifically what has changed for your child's year, rather than assuming the policy describes their experience.

And note that the policy's own stated priority, secure foundational literacy and numeracy, is the thing a family can most directly support at home.
alternative-education-in-india:
What exists in practice, the legal position, and the questions a family should ask before moving a child.

What exists

Montessori, widespread in cities, and with enormous variation in fidelity. The name is not protected, so it ranges from properly trained settings to a conventional preschool with some materials on a shelf.

Waldorf and Steiner schools, present in several cities.

Krishnamurti Foundation schools, a small number of long-established institutions with a distinctive philosophy about learning without fear and without comparison.

Aurobindo and Integral education settings, including Auroville.

Modern gurukul-inspired schools, varying enormously in what they take from the tradition and how carefully.

Democratic and free schools, a small number, where children have substantial say over what they do.

Homeschooling and unschooling networks, growing, particularly in cities.

The legal position

This is what most families need first and find hardest to establish.

The Right to Education Act makes education compulsory for children aged six to fourteen. It is generally understood to place obligations on the state and on schools rather than to prohibit home education, and homeschooling is not explicitly banned.

The practical consequence is that homeschooling operates in a grey area. Families do it, and it is not clearly regulated.

For certification, children typically take examinations through NIOS, the National Institute of Open Schooling, which offers recognised secondary and senior secondary qualifications and is the standard route for home-educated children.

Unrecognised alternative schools may not be able to issue transfer certificates or enter children for board examinations, which matters at the point of transition.

This is general information rather than legal advice, and the position varies by state. Check locally before deciding.

The questions to ask

What are the exits? Can a child move to a conventional school later, and at what point does it become difficult. Can they sit board examinations, and through which route.

Is the school recognised, and does it matter for your plan?

What is the teacher training? Specifically which training, and where.

What happens to a child who is not thriving?

What are the safeguarding arrangements? Smaller and less regulated settings need to be clearer about this, not less.

Who else is here? Fee-paying alternatives often serve a narrow social group.

The honest caution

Fidelity varies more than the label suggests, in every category. A well-run conventional school is better than a poorly-run alternative one, and the philosophy on the website tells you very little.

Visit on an ordinary day, watch the children rather than the tour, and talk to families who have left as well as families who stayed.
homeschooling-in-india-a-parents-guide:
The legal position, the board options, the socialisation question answered honestly, and a realistic account of what it asks of the adults.

Is it legal

The short answer is that it is not prohibited and it is not clearly regulated.

The Right to Education Act makes education compulsory for children aged six to fourteen, and is generally understood to place duties on the state and on schools rather than to ban home education. There is no registration system for homeschoolers and no established enforcement against them.

Families should be aware that this is a grey area rather than a settled right, that interpretations vary, and that the position differs by state.

General information, not legal advice. Check your own state's position before committing.

Certification

This is the practical question that determines everything downstream.

NIOS is the usual route. The National Institute of Open Schooling offers recognised secondary and senior secondary qualifications, accepts private candidates, and is designed for exactly this. Its certification is accepted for higher education in India.

IGCSE and international boards are available as private candidates through registered centres, at considerably higher cost.

CBSE has restricted private candidate entry, so it is not generally a route for home-educated children.

Plan the certification route before starting, not at fifteen.

The socialisation question, honestly

It is the question every homeschooling family is asked and it deserves a straight answer rather than a dismissal.

The concern is not that children will meet nobody. It is that school provides sustained, involuntary contact with a mixed group of peers, including people a child would not choose, and that this is where a good deal of social learning happens.

Homeschooled children can absolutely have rich social lives, and it requires deliberate work: co-ops, clubs, sports, neighbourhood friendships, mixed-age groups. What it does not do by itself is provide the involuntary part.

The evidence base is weak and confounded, because families who homeschool differ in many ways. What can be said is that outcomes depend heavily on how much effort goes into this, and that a family should be honest with itself about whether it is doing that work.

What it actually asks of the adults

The part most under-discussed.

An adult substantially at home, which has income implications. Real time daily, not supervision alongside other work. The capacity to teach subjects you are not confident in, or to buy that in. Administrative work: curriculum, records, examination registration. And considerable social pressure from family and neighbours.

It also asks for honesty about whether it is working, which is harder without external assessment.

Questions to settle before starting

How will you know if this is not working. What is the route back into school, and by when does it close. Which board, and when does registration happen. Who provides the peer group. What happens if the parent doing this becomes unwell or needs to work.

Families who do this well have answered these before starting. Families who struggle usually have not.
